notes.definition: A communicable (infectious) disease is a disease caused by a pathogen that can be passed from one organism to another. Pathogens are microorganisms that cause infectious disease: viruses, bacteria, protists and fungi.
explanation: Pathogens are microorganisms that cause infectious disease. There are four types you need to know: viruses, bacteria, protists and fungi. Pathogens can infect both animals and plants. A disease that can be passed from one individual to another is called communicable or infectious. Non-communicable diseases, such as most cancers and heart disease, cannot be caught from someone else.

Bacteria and viruses can reproduce rapidly once they are inside the body. Bacteria are living cells that divide by splitting in two, so their numbers can double in a short time in the warm, moist, nutrient-rich conditions inside a host. Many bacteria produce poisons called toxins. Toxins damage tissues and make us feel ill, which is why bacterial infections often cause symptoms such as fever and sickness.

Viruses are much smaller than bacteria and are not cells. A virus can only reproduce inside the cells of another organism. It enters a host cell and uses the cell to make many copies of itself. The new viruses then burst out of the cell, damaging or destroying it, and go on to infect more cells. This cell damage causes the symptoms of the disease.

Pathogens are spread in three main ways. Direct contact includes touching an infected individual or their body fluids, sexual contact, and plants touching infected leaves. Water spreads pathogens when people drink or bathe in contaminated water, and when splashing rain carries spores between plants. Air spreads pathogens in droplets from coughs and sneezes, and carries fungal spores on the wind. Some pathogens are also spread in contaminated food or by vectors, which are organisms such as mosquitoes that carry a pathogen from one host to another.

The spread of disease can be reduced or prevented in four main ways. Good hygiene, such as handwashing, disinfecting surfaces, cooking food thoroughly and covering coughs, stops pathogens being passed on. Isolating infected individuals keeps them away from people or plants they could infect. Destroying or controlling vectors, for example killing mosquitoes or removing their breeding sites, breaks the chain of transmission. Vaccination makes people immune so they cannot catch and pass on the disease.
keyFacts: Pathogens are microorganisms that cause infectious disease.
The four types of pathogen are viruses, bacteria, protists and fungi.
Pathogens can infect both plants and animals.
Pathogens are spread by direct contact, by water or by air.
Bacteria and viruses can reproduce rapidly inside the body.
Bacteria may produce toxins that damage tissues and make us feel ill.
Viruses live and reproduce inside cells, causing cell damage.
A vector is an organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another.
Spread is reduced by hygiene, isolating infected individuals, destroying or controlling vectors, and vaccination.
Non-communicable diseases cannot be passed from person to person.

keyTerms.definition: A microorganism that causes infectious disease.
A disease caused by a pathogen that can be spread from one organism to another (also called an infectious disease).
A poison produced by some bacteria that damages tissues and makes us feel ill.
An organism, such as a mosquito, that carries a pathogen from one host to another without usually being harmed by it.
The organism that a pathogen infects and lives in or on.
Keeping an infected individual away from others so the pathogen cannot be passed on.
Practices such as handwashing, disinfecting and cooking food thoroughly that reduce the spread of pathogens.

workedExamples.title: Explaining why a pathogen makes us ill
workedExamples.question: Explain why a bacterial infection and a viral infection both make a person feel ill, even though the pathogens work in different ways.
steps: Both pathogens reproduce rapidly inside the body, so their numbers increase quickly.
Bacteria release toxins, which damage tissues and make us feel ill.
Viruses reproduce inside cells, and the cells are damaged or destroyed when the new viruses are released.
In both cases body tissues are damaged, which causes symptoms.
workedExamples.answer: Both reproduce rapidly; bacteria produce toxins that damage tissues, while viruses damage the cells they reproduce inside.

workedExamples.title: Choosing a control method
workedExamples.question: A disease of farm animals is spread by flies that carry the pathogen from animal to animal. Suggest two ways a farmer could reduce the spread and explain each.
steps: Identify the route: the flies are vectors.
Method 1: control the vector, for example spray insecticide or remove dung and standing water where flies breed. Fewer flies means fewer animals bitten.
Method 2: isolate infected animals in a separate building. Flies are then less likely to carry the pathogen from infected to healthy animals.
Other valid answers: vaccinate the animals if a vaccine exists.
workedExamples.answer: Control the flies (vector) so fewer carry the pathogen; isolate infected animals so the pathogen is not carried to healthy ones.

workedExamples.title: Bacterial growth calculation
workedExamples.question: A single bacterium enters a wound. It divides once every 20 minutes. How many bacteria will there be after 2 hours, assuming none die?
steps: Number of divisions = 120 minutes ÷ 20 minutes = 6 divisions.
Each division doubles the number, so number = 1 × 2⁶.
workedExamples.answer: 64 bacteria. This shows how rapidly bacteria can reproduce inside the body.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all microorganisms are pathogens.
misconceptions.right: In fact most microorganisms are harmless or useful. Only those that cause infectious disease are called pathogens.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think viruses are tiny bacteria and can be grown on their own.
misconceptions.right: In fact viruses are not cells at all. They can only reproduce inside the living cells of a host.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think bacteria make us ill just by being in the body.
misconceptions.right: In fact bacteria make us feel ill mainly because many of them produce toxins that damage tissues.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think only animals get communicable diseases.
misconceptions.right: In fact plants are infected by pathogens too, for example tobacco mosaic virus and rose black spot.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a vector is the pathogen itself.
misconceptions.right: In fact a vector, such as a mosquito, only carries the pathogen. The pathogen in malaria is a protist.

realWorld: Hospitals reduce the spread of infections by hand gel at every ward entrance, isolation rooms and strict cleaning of surfaces.
Public health campaigns such as 'Catch it, bin it, kill it' encourage people to cover coughs and sneezes to reduce airborne spread.
Farmers and gardeners remove and burn infected plant material to stop spores and viruses spreading to healthy crops.
Clean drinking water and sewage treatment have greatly reduced waterborne diseases in many countries.
examTips: When asked how a disease is spread, name the route precisely (for example 'droplets from coughs and sneezes in the air'), not just 'it is catching'.
For 'explain how spread can be reduced' questions, link each method to the route: hygiene, isolation, vector control or vaccination, and say why it works.
Keep bacteria and viruses separate: bacteria produce toxins; viruses damage cells by reproducing inside them.
Do not write 'germs' in an exam. Use the word pathogen and name the type (virus, bacterium, protist or fungus).
summary: Pathogens are microorganisms that cause infectious disease: viruses, bacteria, protists and fungi.
Pathogens infect plants and animals and spread by direct contact, water or air (and in food or by vectors).
Bacteria and viruses reproduce rapidly inside the body.
Bacteria may produce toxins that damage tissues; viruses damage the cells they reproduce in.
Spread is reduced by hygiene, isolation, controlling vectors and vaccination.

flashcards.back: A microorganism that causes infectious disease.

flashcards.front: Name the four types of pathogen.
What are the three main ways pathogens are spread?
How do bacteria make us feel ill?
flashcards.back: They reproduce rapidly and may produce toxins (poisons) that damage tissues.
They live and reproduce inside cells, damaging or destroying the cells.
An organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another, for example a mosquito.
A disease caused by a pathogen that can be passed from one organism to another.

flashcards.front: Give four ways to reduce or prevent the spread of disease.
flashcards.back: Hygiene, isolating infected individuals, destroying or controlling vectors, and vaccination.

flashcards.front: Can plants be infected by pathogens?
flashcards.back: Yes. Examples are tobacco mosaic virus (virus) and rose black spot (fungus).

flashcards.front: Why does handwashing reduce the spread of disease?
flashcards.back: It removes pathogens from the hands so they are not passed on by direct contact or onto food.

flashcards.front: Why can viruses not be treated in the same way as bacteria?
flashcards.back: Viruses live inside host cells, so it is hard to kill them without damaging the cells.

flashcards.front: How does isolating an infected person reduce spread?
flashcards.back: It prevents contact with healthy people, so the pathogen cannot be passed on.

questions.question: What is a pathogen?
options: A microorganism that causes infectious disease
A white blood cell that destroys microorganisms
markScheme: 1 mark: a microorganism that causes infectious disease
questions.explanation: A pathogen is specifically a microorganism that causes infectious disease. Most microorganisms are not pathogens. A chemical that kills bacteria is an antibiotic or disinfectant, and white blood cells defend against pathogens.

questions.question: Which list contains only types of pathogen?
markScheme: 1 mark: viruses, bacteria, protists, fungi
questions.explanation: The four types of pathogen are viruses, bacteria, protists and fungi. Vectors carry pathogens, toxins are poisons made by bacteria and antibodies are made by white blood cells; none of these are pathogens.

questions.question: Measles is spread when people breathe in droplets from an infected person's coughs and sneezes. Which route of transmission is this?
markScheme: 1 mark: air
questions.explanation: Droplets from coughs and sneezes travel through the air and are inhaled, so this is airborne spread. Direct contact would involve touching, and no vector organism is involved.

questions.question: Why do many bacterial infections make people feel ill?
options: Bacteria reproduce inside body cells and burst them
Bacteria use up all the oxygen in the blood
Bacteria produce toxins that damage tissues
Bacteria destroy all of the white blood cells
markScheme: 1 mark: bacteria produce toxins that damage tissues
questions.explanation: Many bacteria produce toxins (poisons) that damage tissues and make us feel ill. Reproducing inside cells and bursting them describes viruses, not bacteria.

questions.question: Which statement about viruses is correct?
options: Viruses reproduce only inside living cells
Viruses are single-celled organisms with a nucleus
markScheme: 1 mark: viruses reproduce only inside living cells
questions.explanation: Viruses are not cells; they can only reproduce inside the cells of a host, damaging those cells. They are much smaller than bacteria and infect plants as well as animals (for example tobacco mosaic virus).

questions.question: Which of these is a vector?
options: A mosquito that carries the malaria protist
A doctor treating a patient with malaria
markScheme: 1 mark: a mosquito that carries the malaria protist
questions.explanation: A vector is an organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another. The protist is the pathogen itself, not the vector. A mosquito net is a way of avoiding the vector.

questions.question: A gardener notices a plant with a viral disease. Which action would best reduce the spread of the virus to other plants?
options: Watering the infected plant more often
Removing and destroying the infected plant
Moving the infected plant closer to healthy plants
markScheme: 1 mark: removing and destroying the infected plant
questions.explanation: Removing and destroying the infected plant isolates the source of the pathogen so it cannot reach healthy plants by contact. Watering and fertiliser do not stop spread, and moving plants closer would increase spread by direct contact.

questions.question: Which method of reducing disease spread works by breaking the link between an infected host and a new host through an animal carrier?
markScheme: 1 mark: controlling vectors
questions.explanation: Vectors are animal carriers of pathogens, so destroying or controlling vectors breaks this link. Vaccination makes individuals immune, isolation separates infected individuals, and cooking kills pathogens in food.

questions.question: Bacteria and viruses can both reproduce rapidly inside the body. Which statement best explains why viral infections cause tissue damage?
options: Viruses release enzymes that digest the outside of cells
Viruses reproduce inside host cells, and the cells are damaged when new viruses are released
Viruses produce toxins in the same way as all bacteria
Viruses take glucose from the blood so that cells starve
markScheme: 1 mark: viruses reproduce inside host cells, damaging cells when released
questions.explanation: Viruses take over host cells to make copies of themselves; the cell is damaged or destroyed when the new viruses leave. Toxin production is the way bacteria cause damage.

questions.question: A new disease spreads rapidly in a crowded city. Scientists find that the pathogen is carried in droplets but also survives for days on door handles. Which combination of measures would be most effective?
options: Covering coughs, handwashing and cleaning surfaces
Removing standing water and draining ponds
markScheme: 1 mark: covering coughs, handwashing and cleaning surfaces
questions.explanation: The pathogen spreads by air (droplets) and by touching contaminated surfaces. Covering coughs targets airborne droplets; handwashing and cleaning surfaces target direct and indirect contact. Nets, insecticide and draining ponds target insect vectors, and boiling water targets waterborne pathogens.

questions.question: A bacterium divides once every 20 minutes inside a wound. Starting with one bacterium, how many bacteria will there be after 3 hours, assuming none die?
markScheme: 1 mark: number of divisions = 180 ÷ 20 = 9
1 mark: 2⁹ = 512
questions.explanation: 3 hours is 180 minutes, so there are 180 ÷ 20 = 9 divisions. The number doubles each time: 1 × 2⁹ = 512. A common error is to multiply 9 × 2 = 18, which ignores that the population doubles each generation.

questions.question: In a school of 1250 students, 75 students caught a communicable disease during one term. Calculate the percentage of students who caught the disease.
questions.explanation: Percentage = (number infected ÷ total) × 100 = (75 ÷ 1250) × 100 = 6%.

questions.question: A hospital ward recorded 250 infections in a year. After hand gel was placed at every bed, the number fell to 160 infections the next year. Calculate the percentage decrease in infections.
markScheme: 1 mark: decrease = 250 − 160 = 90
questions.explanation: Percentage change is always calculated from the original value: 90 ÷ 250 × 100 = 36%. Dividing by 160 instead gives 56.25%, which is wrong because 160 is the new value.

questions.question: A bacterial population inside a host doubles every 30 minutes. An infection starts with 200 bacteria. How many hours will it take for the population to reach 51 200 bacteria?
markScheme: 1 mark: 256 = 2⁸, so 8 doublings
1 mark: 8 × 30 minutes = 240 minutes = 4 hours
questions.explanation: The population must increase by a factor of 51 200 ÷ 200 = 256. Since 2⁸ = 256, eight doublings are needed. Eight doublings × 30 minutes = 240 minutes, which is 4 hours.

questions.question: State what is meant by a communicable disease.
acceptedAnswers: disease that can be spread/passed from one organism/person to another
markScheme: 1 mark: a disease (caused by a pathogen) that can be passed from one organism to another
questions.explanation: Communicable means 'can be communicated', so the disease can be transmitted between individuals. It is caused by a pathogen.

questions.question: Name three ways in which pathogens can be spread.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any three: direct contact; water; air (droplets); vectors; contaminated food
questions.explanation: The specification names direct contact, water and air. Vectors and contaminated food are also accepted routes.

questions.question: Describe how a virus causes damage to the body.
markScheme: 1 mark: virus enters (host) cells and reproduces inside them
1 mark: the cells are damaged or destroyed (when new viruses are released)
questions.explanation: Viruses live and reproduce inside cells. When the new virus particles leave, the cell is damaged or destroyed, causing symptoms.

questions.question: Explain why washing hands before preparing food reduces the spread of disease.
markScheme: 1 mark: removes or kills pathogens on the hands
1 mark: so pathogens are not transferred to food and ingested by others
questions.explanation: Hands pick up pathogens by contact. Washing removes them, so they cannot be passed onto food and then eaten.

questions.question: Explain why isolating a patient with an infectious disease reduces the spread of the disease.
acceptedAnswers: cannot spread by air/contact to others
markScheme: 1 mark: the patient has less or no contact with healthy people
1 mark: so the pathogen cannot be passed on to them
questions.explanation: Isolation removes the opportunity for the pathogen to reach new hosts, whether by contact or by droplets in the air.

questions.question: Give one way in which pathogens are spread between plants.
markScheme: 1 mark: wind/air, water/rain splash, direct contact between plants, or insect vectors
questions.explanation: Plant pathogens are spread by wind and water (for example fungal spores), direct contact between leaves, and by insects acting as vectors.

questions.question: Suggest why diseases spread more quickly in crowded cities than in rural areas. Explain your answer.
markScheme: 1 mark: people are closer together or have more contact
1 mark: so droplets in the air or direct contact reach more people
1 mark: each infected person can infect more others, so the number of cases rises faster (or: shared facilities/poorer sanitation increase spread)
questions.explanation: Spread needs contact between an infected and a healthy host. In crowded places each infected person meets more people, so airborne and contact transmission happens more often and cases multiply faster.

questions.question: Suggest why it is harder to develop drugs that kill viruses than drugs that kill bacteria.
markScheme: 1 mark: viruses live and reproduce inside host cells
1 mark: so a drug that destroys the virus may also damage the body's own cells
questions.explanation: Bacteria are separate cells that can be targeted without harming body cells. Viruses use the host cell's own machinery, so it is difficult to destroy them without harming the cell.

questions.question: State two ways that good hygiene can reduce the spread of disease.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: washing hands; disinfecting surfaces or equipment; cooking food thoroughly; covering mouth when coughing or sneezing; keeping animals out of food areas
questions.explanation: Hygiene measures remove or kill pathogens before they can reach a new host.

questions.question: A student says, 'Bacteria and viruses cause disease in exactly the same way.' Give one way in which they are different in how they cause disease.
markScheme: 1 mark: bacteria (may) produce toxins that damage tissues
1 mark: viruses reproduce inside cells, causing cell damage
questions.explanation: Both reproduce rapidly, but bacteria mainly cause harm through toxins, while viruses damage the cells they reproduce inside.

questions.question: Describe how bacteria and viruses cause disease once they are inside the body.
markScheme: Indicative content: both bacteria and viruses reproduce rapidly inside the body; bacteria are cells that divide; bacteria may produce toxins (poisons); toxins damage tissues and make us feel ill; viruses enter cells; viruses reproduce inside cells; cells are damaged or destroyed when viruses are released; new viruses infect more cells.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear description of how both bacteria and viruses cause disease, including toxins and cell damage.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about one type of pathogen, or both with little detail.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: A full answer covers rapid reproduction for both, toxins for bacteria and reproduction inside cells causing cell damage for viruses.

questions.question:
A new communicable disease appears in a town. It spreads in droplets from coughs and sneezes, by touching contaminated surfaces, and some cases are linked to flies landing on food.
Explain the measures that health officials could use to reduce the spread of this disease.
markScheme: Indicative content: airborne route: covering mouth and nose, using tissues, wearing masks, ventilation; contact route: handwashing, disinfecting surfaces, avoiding shared items; vector route: controlling flies with insecticide or removing breeding sites such as rubbish, covering food; isolating infected people so they cannot pass on the pathogen; vaccination (if a vaccine is developed) so people become immune and cannot be infected or pass it on; each measure linked to breaking a route of transmission.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): several measures covering at least three of: hygiene, isolation, vector control, vaccination; each clearly linked to the route of transmission it blocks.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): several measures given with some explanation of how they reduce spread.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two measures with little or no explanation.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Top answers match each route to a control method and explain how it prevents the pathogen reaching a new host: hygiene for droplets and contact, controlling the flies as vectors, isolating the infected and vaccination.

questions.question: Compare how pathogens are spread in plants and in animals. Use examples in your answer.
markScheme: Indicative content: both can be spread by direct contact (sexual contact or touching in animals; leaves touching in plants, for example tobacco mosaic virus); both by water (contaminated drinking water in animals; rain splash spreading spores in plants, for example rose black spot); both by air (droplets from coughs and sneezes in animals, for example measles; spores carried by wind in plants); vectors (mosquitoes for malaria in animals; insects in plants); animals can also be infected via contaminated food (Salmonella).
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear comparison with similarities and/or differences and relevant examples for both plants and animals.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): routes described for plants or animals with limited comparison.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Compare means give similarities and differences. The same three main routes apply to both, but the details differ: droplets versus spores in air, drinking water versus rain splash.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a way of reducing the spread of a communicable disease?
markScheme: 1 mark: sharing drinking cups
questions.explanation: Sharing cups allows pathogens to pass by direct contact with saliva, so it increases spread. The other three are standard ways of reducing spread.
